posts.text: That is a great question. The set was originally expected to retire in 2027, so it was shorten not for one but for two years. They would not do that, if it was selling very well, so it is most probable that it actually was not. Why would that be the case? It is hard to say and probably it is a combination of various factors. First, maybe because it is not castle. I love civilian buildings, but it seems that people on average prefer castles in Castle theme. Although medieval market village was a hit back in the day, so that probably is not the main reason. Second, maybe because it was not that good. We had preliminary pictures for the set, that were better and had more minifigs and more animals. The finished product was somewhat stripped down, had too much stickers and maybe some people were dissapointed. Maybe they saw it as nothing special and too expensive for what it was. Third, maybe people lost interest. They already bough the castle and then the BDP sets were coming and noone was buying this set. 2024 brought us Medieval Town Square, Mountain Fortress, Forest Stronghold and of course Lion Knights Castle was still available, soon to be retired, so people with limited budget maybe saw this set as the weakest. Of course there is a small possibility that the sales were average and that they retired it for some other reason. Maybe it was linked too much to the castle and they expected it not to do well as a stand alone product. However I would say that probably it was not so popular form the start. posts.title: Using Claude AI for new ports and translations
posts.text: https://htmlhoster.com/p/BZYFKCBZ/ Claude wrote: "I've added an emulation of the missing LEGO TC Controller to the editor (Version 18). The book shows it was software, not a separate box. It was a resident program called CONTROL.EXE, with a keyboard "direct control" window and a Turbo Pascal unit called LTCC. I rebuilt both from the book's descriptions, so the details are not guaranteed to match the original. I tested it with scripted keystrokes and a simulated serial device, not a real Interface A. The new code is in the page, the Pascal editor mode and the Interface A panel. Direct control: a new "Direct control" button opens a window in the Interface A panel, styled after the book's figure 7.3. The keys follow the book: Keys 0–5 toggle outputs. The arrow keys drive motors A and B, and PgUp/PgDn drive C. Space switches everything off. Shift-right plus a key raises a power level, 0–8, and Shift-left lowers it. Counters A and B reset with the 6 and 7 keys, and Esc closes the window. Every button also works by click. A "last instruction" line shows the Pascal command that matches what you pressed. LTCC unit: in the Pascal mode, uses LTCC; now gives you the unit's full procedure list: BitOn, Motor, SetPower, the flash, counter, clock and timer calls, Wait and ResetController. Without that line you get the same "Unknown identifier" error as in Turbo Pascal. There are five new examples: a running light power levels frequency and counters flash and timer counting turns Power levels: with the real Interface A connected, levels 1–7 are produced by pulsing the outputs. I tested that against the simulated serial device only. Level 4 gave half on and half off. Counters in simulation: a "Virtual count disc" checkbox, on by default, makes a simulated disc on motors A and B feed inputs 6 and 7. I calibrated it so the frequency example gives 142 Hz, as in the book. The counter reading was 573 against the book's 564. The Direct procedure only prints a note during a simulated run, because the window can't take over a running program. The motor mode names in the book are only partly legible, so I accept lft, rgt, trn and hlt, plus the English words left, right, toggle and halt. Should I add a second interface at address 926 next? The book says the card can be jumpered to it, and the TC Controller had a matching second-interface variant (CONTROL2 and LTCC2, opened with Alt-J)."

You and me for sure... ;-) ) Generic ESP32 device bridge for LB needs some engineering to make it as simple as possible and versatile (to handle many type of sensors, neopixel, IR, VLL LED, H Bridge with PWM, etc) and develop a "standard" protocol etc... So a generic LB ESP32 device is not for tomorrow but eventually, I might come up with something. That reminds me the famous TASMOTA (ESP) project for smart home that is an ongoing project since many years and has a big community. This project is BIG and is a good example of support for many type of sensors (Switches, Temperature, Illuminance etc) and output devices (H-Bridge, Leds, OLED etc). You access the ESP32 webpage to configure which GPIO does what and the Code handle all the sensors logic, protocol, etc... Very complex and I don't want to go into that complexity all alone since LB has a very small audience. Unfortunately, Tasmota firmware is primarily built for a Wifi use. Which is good for local network but Lego Blockly is a Web App using HTTPS which makes it very difficult to interact with local Wifi (Security issues). This is a limitation of LB. I cannot use easily the Wifi capability of the ESP32 which is its main strength... Unless I make LB a local HTTP app which would break one goal of blockly, to be accessible from the WEB and get new versions automatically. Thanks again for your enthousiasm over LB!

posts.title: [WIP] Jamestown: A Colonial Redcoat Capital
posts.text: Jamestown Here is a project I’ve slowly been piecing together for over a year now with some contribution from my son. Jamestown is a highly fictionalized version of the first permanent English colony in North America, (not surprisingly) named Jamestown. The actual Jamestown was established in 1607 but eventually faded away in favor of nearby Williamsburg, which became the capital of Virginia in 1699. Both are located about an hour away from where I live. This display is based off a combination of both Jamestown and Williamsburg and geographically set in that general area. If one is predisposed to locations closer to “big water” this display can easily be imagined as an early version of Norfolk, Virginia. The display itself is baseplate based. It’s 3x3 32x32 stud baseplates for a total of nine plates. Five of these are green and four are blue. The design is simple. It is not meant to be as detailed and elaborate as some of the MOCs I’ve seen posted here. With that said, I do intend to keep evolving it, adding details to the buildings (inside and out). I don’t want it to become too elaborate though. It’s supposed to fit right in with the vintage Imperial Redcoats I love so much. And by extension the vintage pirates theme overall. With this in mind, the sand is “bright yellow” and the water is the basic blue of those old baseplates. I always felt like the one thing the theme was missing was civilians just living their lives. The Islanders sort of addressed this, but there still were no imperial civilians. Jamestown is my biggest attempt to address that gap. This post about Jamestown is also the first out of several I will share intended to weave my own lore into the actual displays I’ve built. It’s amazing to me how combining sets can lead to imaginative storytelling, even for a grown adult who never fully outgrew his love for vintage Lego pirates! With that in mind it was important to me to integrate some of the original vintage sets into it. I didn’t use any software applications to design this display; I just studied a few pics of what early 18th century waterfront communities may have looked like and tried to match what I saw. I do love these new “brick” bricks, which weren’t available when the original waves were introduced. I think even in a simple design like this they really do give it some good texture. I also made sure to do some buildings in plain white brick, again to help “phase” the overall aesthetic with the vintage stuff. When we first started building, my son and I went back and forth between naming it Jamestown or Williamsburg, which eventually emerged as the colonial capital of Virginia. We decided on Jamestown for a few reasons. One, it’s a riverfront display, and Jamestown was built on the banks of the James River while Williamsburg is inland a couple miles. We also just like the historic Jamestown site quite a bit more than Colonial Williamsburg. Truthfully, if you are on this forum and your interest in Lego Pirates can be even loosely tied to the Age of Sail, North American and Caribbean colonial history, and the people who lived in these eras, you can’t go wrong with either location. With my Lego displays I’m not a stickler for historical accuracy. I’ll place my displays somewhere between 1715 and 1725. posts.title: Wet Winds - an RC windmill building operation
posts.text: Together with the talented Appie we entertained the visitors of Legoworld Utrecht with a windmill building operation this year. The goal is to set up a windmill completely remotely controlled, without any manual help. This is done with massive crane barges, pulled along with tugboats. The parts for the windmills are supplied on separate barges. The building operation runs on two Powered Up hubs each, one for the tugboat and one for the crane. The windmills use Power Functions. Brickcontroller2 and Pybricks were used to control the MOCs. Even though the windmill designs and construction are radically different, we found that construction time per windmill was remarkably similar. Maybe a fun challenge for others to try? We're convinced there are way more possibilities for other designs.

posts.title: Using Claude AI for new ports and translations
posts.text: @Toastie Here is Claude reply and the new simulator. https://htmlhoster.com/p/D0EKBC10/ Hi Toastie, thanks for testing it and for the great questions! **Turtle window in BASIC mode.** You're right, it isn't needed there. At the moment the preview panel is shared by all modes, but I can hide it in BASIC (and let you swap its place with the Interface A panel, or toggle each panel). Each panel already has a full-screen button. **Which BASIC?** None in particular. It is my own interpreter written in JavaScript, not an emulator. It accepts the common GW-BASIC / QuickBASIC / Turbo Basic style (line numbers or labels, PRINT, FOR/NEXT, IF/THEN, `OUT 925, n`, `INP(925)`), so typical Interface A listings should run. A text/graphics switch for BASIC output is a good idea and I'll look at it. **Interface A at 925 (&H39D).** Yes, that is what the virtual Interface A panel shows: outputs 0 to 5 as red lamps, inputs 6 and 7 as green lamps you can click like sensors, motor pairs A/B/C, and the byte a program would send with `OUT 925`. I have not emulated any other hardware yet. **Real hardware.** This is the tricky part. The Interface A is not serial: it is 8 parallel bits (6 outputs, 2 inputs) at one I/O address, so a COM port can't drive it directly. A browser page can't reach an ISA card either. The realistic routes are (1) a small bridge, either a microcontroller (Arduino/ESP32 style) that behaves like the interface, or something like the TC Logo Connect USB-C bridge, plus a local copy of the page using Web Serial/WebUSB, or (2) just exporting files for the original software on a real PC with the ISA card. For (2) the editor already exports TC Logo pages (.LWR) and LEGO Lines programs (.LIN, the real format from the original disk), so you can prepare programs in the browser and run them on real hardware. If anyone knows the protocol of the USB bridges being developed here, I'd be glad to hook the editor to them. **Use cases for visitors.** Mainly to let people try TC Logo, BASIC and LEGO Lines without owning the old hardware or software, and to share programs. The editor also converts the primitives between English, French, Spanish and Portuguese. Other recent additions: a LEGO Lines mode with an editable sequencer table (with .LIN import/export), colour-coded code with automatic indentation, a command center, and a command line for single commands. Thanks again, and glad you like it! Claude AI -
